own_scenes.desc: El revival folk de finales de los cincuenta lo habían moldeado comunistas como Ewan MacColl y Bert Lloyd, para quienes el folk era escritura sagrada de la clase obrera. La nueva generación, nacida durante o justo después de la guerra, vivía la vida: viajaba, okupaba y tocaba en una red de clubes pequeños. Su figura de transición fue Davy Graham, cuya «Angi» (1962) se volvió el estándar de los guitarristas acústicos y que introdujo la afinación DADGAD para imitar el oud que oyó en Marruecos. Les Cousins, abierto en Greek Street el 16 de abril de 1965 como club de toda la noche, fue refugio de fugados y adolescentes de suburbio y semillero de Bert Jansch, Paul Simon, Jackson C. Frank, Roy Harper, Donovan, Sandy Denny, Mick Softley y Anne Briggs: romanticismo maldito, sin temas tabú (prostitución masculina, heroína, salud mental). La trabajadora social Judith Piepe acogía en su piso de Cable Street a Simon, Al Stewart, Denny y Frank.

refs.q: The folkies found a home at Les Cousins, which opened on 16 April 1965 in Greek Street
refs.para: The folkies found a home at Les Cousins, which opened on 16 April 1965 in Greek Street, at the centre of London’s Soho. This was still an interzone in the heart of the capital, a district for dissipation, excess and desperation – all the facets of bohemianism. Whether intentionally or not, the club, as the folk historian Colin Harper notes, marked ‘the line in the sand between the old order of folk song epitomised by Ewan MacColl and his left-wing agenda and the new dis-order of individual folk singers’.
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: This was a new kind of romanticism: anti-pop although soon to become pop
refs.para: This was a new kind of romanticism: anti-pop although soon to become pop, weighed down with the cares of the world yet soon to trip into inner space. No subject was taboo in the repertoire of the Les Cousins regulars: there were songs about male prostitution (Al Stewart’s ‘Pretty Golden Hair’), drug addiction (Bert Jansch’s ‘Needle of Death’), isolation (Paul Simon’s ‘I Am a Rock’), mental-health policy (Roy Harper’s ‘Committed’), as well as the haunting visions of Jackson C. Frank’s ‘Carnival’ and ‘Blues Run the Game’.
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: The music of ‘The War Drags On’ is relentless
refs.para: The music of ‘The War Drags On’ is relentless: the bottom string is held to a D chord, providing a sombre drone that, in its obdurate stasis, commands the attention. This was partly a matter of practicality. In folk clubs, a solo performer with an acoustic guitar had to find a way of filling out the sound. Holding a drone chord enabled the player to make chord changes on the other strings and thus effectively do the job of two musicians. It also said, ‘I am resolute. I am not trying to please.’
